[EMERGING] A humanoid robot on scooter wheels just landed a 360° spin jump on its first real attempt. 🛼

Boston Dynamics bolted wheels onto its Atlas humanoid with a single custom adapter and modeled each wheel as an ankle that spins forever. A whole-body controller trained with reinforcement learning across millions of simulated runs figured out rolling on its own, then transferred to the real robot. The company released the video on Nov. 9.

Reality check: Boston Dynamics says a wheeled Atlas is a research testbed, not a product. The goal was to push its motors to their limits and make simulation match real hardware. Lessons are already flowing back into the standard, legged Atlas.

[EMERGING] How do you teach a robot to do laundry? Steer it yourself first. 🤖

Think of a driving instructor with dual controls. In Korea's new AI Humanoid Data Factory, opened Nov. 3 by the research institutes KIMM and ETRI, people remotely control 12 humanoid robots through tasks like taking items out of a fridge, handling laundry or pressing buttons inside a car. The robots' movements are recorded and used to train AI.

The trained AI then runs on real robots, and the new data from those tests feeds the next round of training. The goal is AI that works across different robot bodies.

Reality check: this is a research facility, not robots in homes. KIMM plans to open it to industry and universities gradually from the end of 2027.

[IMAGINE] What if a warehouse robot learned its best move in a building it has never seen? 📦

What is real: GXO and Agility Robotics say Digit humanoids have moved more than 100,000 totes at a GXO warehouse in Flowery Branch, Georgia, working alongside existing automation. On Oct. 26 the companies announced Digit will start at GXO sites in Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee, in early 2027. Agility reports more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation and runs a cloud platform for managing robot fleets. These are company figures.

The speculation: as fleets grow, a skill learned at one site might be shared with robots everywhere. That raises real questions about safety checks, customer data and who owns what a robot learns.

[TODAY] Four years after humanity punched an asteroid, a detective has arrived at the scene. 🔭

ESA's Hera spacecraft released its first close-up of the Didymos system on Nov. 5, taken from about 60 km away. The 780-meter asteroid Didymos shows a ridge around its equator, many boulders and craters, and patterns that may be grooves or ridges. Its 151-meter moon Dimorphos, the target NASA's DART spacecraft struck in 2022, sits mostly in shadow. That impact shortened the moon's orbit by about 33 minutes.

Reality check: ESA's mission scientist says some features may come from impact debris that crossed the roughly 1 km gap, but that still has to be worked out. ESA plans to release detailed images on Nov. 25.

[TODAY] If you say hello to Voyager 1 next week, the answer will take two days to come back. 📡

On Nov. 18, NASA's Voyager 1 will be 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion km) from Earth. That's one light-day: the distance light travels in 24 hours. Radio signals move at the speed of light, so a command takes a day to arrive and the reply takes another day. Think of a letter that needs a full day each way.

No human-made object has ever been this far. Launched in 1977, the probe is moving at about 38,000 mph and loses roughly 4 watts of power every year, so engineers keep switching off what it doesn't need.

Reality check: crossing the line changes nothing on the spacecraft. It's a milestone for us, a measure of how big space is.

[IMAGINE] What if the biggest telescope ever never had to fit inside a rocket? 🛰️

What is real: Caltech says its ASTRA robot, funded by DARPA, built part of a structure in space without astronauts, a first. Launched on March 30, it carried two prebuilt sections of an antenna frame and assembled a third in low Earth orbit, with engineers sending commands during short daily contact windows.

Reality check: the planned dish is only 1.4 meters across and needs 11 sections. The team says it is unlikely to finish before the mission ends in December, but the method looks workable.

The speculation: today, size is capped by the rocket's nose cone. Robots assembling parts in orbit could one day build mirrors, antennas or solar arrays far bigger than any launch.

[EMERGING] For nearly 90 years, magnets came in two families. Physicists now say there is a third. 🧲

A team led by SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory reports in Science robust experimental confirmation of altermagnetism. Using circularly polarized X-rays in France, they found a 'handedness' (chirality), like the twist of a spiral staircase, in manganese telluride, a material long filed as an ordinary antiferromagnet.

Why it matters: ferromagnets carry information but are easy to disturb with a stray magnet. Antiferromagnets are stable but hard to read. Altermagnets have zero net magnetization yet can still produce spin-polarized currents, a potential fit for spin-based memory and more efficient data centers.

Reality check: this is fundamental research. The next step is learning to control these states with light and electricity, and significant development is still needed.

[EMERGING] Imagine ice that keeps its crystal shape but flows without any friction. Physicists just made that at room temperature. ❄️

That strange state is called a supersolid: the orderly pattern of a crystal combined with the frictionless flow of a superfluid. It was first observed in 2017 in clouds of atoms cooled to near absolute zero. Now a team from the University of Warsaw, Poland's Military University of Technology, IBM Research Zurich and France's CNRS made one from exciton polaritons, hybrid particles of light and matter, inside a tiny liquid-crystal optical chamber. The device can also be tuned with electricity. The work appears in Science Advances.

Reality check: the samples lasted only a few hours before degrading. Light-based computing and sensors are possibilities for future research, not near products.

Sources (link in bio):
University of Warsaw via ScienceDaily, Nov. 9, 2026, "A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid"
